headline: RFC 9110 Defines 402 Payment Required Only as 'Reserved for Future Use'
summary: The supplied excerpt of RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics, June 2022) states in Section 15.5.3 that the 402 (Payment Required) status code 'is reserved for future use' [1]. The same document lists 402 in its status-code summary table with the description 'Payment Required' and a pointer to Section 15.5.3 [1]. The excerpt contains no definition of a payment mechanism, no wire format, and no mention of any modern payment protocol or vendor implementation [1]. Because only one source is supplied and it is the publisher's own text, any claim that 402 is standardized for a specific payment scheme or supported by particular software is not supported by these excerpts [1].
body: The assignment asked what RFC 9110 actually specifies for HTTP 402. The only supplied source is the RFC text itself, fetched from rfc-editor.org, and the publisher's text is treated as a claim rather than independent corroboration [1].

In the excerpt covering Section 15.5.3, the entire normative text for 402 is: 'The 402 (Payment Required) status code is reserved for future use.' [1] That is the full specification of the code's semantics in the supplied material.

The status-code summary table in the excerpt lists '402 | Payment Required | 15.5.3', confirming the code number, its reason phrase, and the section that defines it [1]. The table entry adds no further semantics beyond the section text.

The excerpt does not describe any payment protocol, header field, token, challenge, or message format associated with 402, and it does not name any vendor, product, or implementation [1]. Claims that 402 is standardized for a particular modern payment scheme, or that specific software supports it, cannot be verified from these excerpts and should be attributed to whoever makes them, not to RFC 9110.

The excerpt is explicitly marked as truncated and omits large portions of the document [1]. It is therefore possible that related material exists elsewhere in RFC 9110 that is not visible here; the absence of such material in the excerpt is not proof of its absence in the full document.

No supplementary research was purchased because the assignment budget was below the quoted cost, so no second source is available to cross-check the RFC text or to test claims about modern payment protocols [1].

[Excerpt at character 320000] t Error 4xx The 4xx (Client Error) class of status code indicates that the client seems to have erred. Except when responding to a HEAD request, the server SHOULD send a representation containing an explanation of the error situation, and whether it is a temporary or permanent condition. These status codes are applicable to any request method. User agents SHOULD display any included representation to the user. 15.5.1. 400 Bad Request The 400 (Bad Request) status code indicates that the server cannot or will not process the request due to something that is perceived to be a client error (e.g., malformed request syntax, invalid request message framing, or deceptive request routing). 15.5.2. 401 Unauthorized The 401 (Unauthorized) status code indicates that the request has not been applied because it lacks valid authentication credentials for the target resource. The server generating a 401 response MUST send a WWW-Authenticate header field (Section 11.6.1) containing at least one challenge applicable to the target resource. If the request included authentication credentials, then the 401 response indicates that authorization has been refused for those credentials. The user agent MAY repeat the request with a new or replaced Authorization header field (Section 11.6.2). If the 401 response contains the same challenge as the prior response, and the user agent has already attempted authentication at least once, then the user agent SHOULD present the enclosed representation to the user, since it usually contains relevant diagnostic information. 15.5.3. 402 Payment Required The 402 (Payment Required) status code is reserved for future use. 15.5.4. 403 Forbidden The 403 (Forbidden) status code indicates that the server understood the request but refuses to fulfill it. A server that wishes to make public why the request has been forbidden can describe that reason in the response content (if any). If authentication credentials were provided in the request, the server considers them insufficient to grant access. The client SHOULD NOT automatically repeat the request with the same credentials. Field Name Registration This specification updates the HTTP-related aspects of the existing registration procedures for message header fields defined in [RFC3864]. It replaces the old procedures as they relate to HTTP by defining a new registration procedure and moving HTTP field definitions into a separate registry. IANA has created a new registry titled "Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) Field Name Registry" as outlined in Section 16.3.1. IANA has moved all entries in the "Permanent Message Header Field Names" and "Provisional Message Header Field Names" registries (see ) with the protocol 'http' to this registry and has applied the following changes: 1. The 'Applicable Protocol' field has been omitted. 2. Entries that had a status of 'standard', 'experimental', 'reserved', or 'informational' have been made to have a status of 'permanent'. 3. Provisional entries without a status have been made to have a status of 'provisional'. 4. Permanent entries without a status (after confirmation that the registration document did not define one) have been made to have a status of 'provisional'. The expert(s) can choose to update the entries' status if there is evidence that another is more appropriate.
